Archive item 3: Aldercroft & District Water Authority – Operations Manual
Source format: Operations Manual

1.1 This volume covers the following assets and activities:
- Cranwell TW Chlorination Unit (including duty/standby dosing pumps, chlorine bulk storage, and injection points).
- Satellite re-chlorination points at Aldercroft Hill, Lower Brampton, and the Marsh Lane booster.
- Manual chlorine residual testing (DPD method) at sample points throughout the distribution network.
- Calibration and verification of on-line chlorine analysers.
- Emergency procedures for loss of chlorination, chlorine gas escape, and contamination events.

1.3 For the purposes of this manual, "chlorine residual" refers to free chlorine, measured as mg/L, unless otherwise stated. Combined chlorine residuals are recorded separately and are not used for setpoint compliance.

2. References and Associated Documents

2.1 The following documents are referenced in this volume:
- S03/OM/001 – Operations Manual Volume 1: General Duties & Safety.
- S03/OM/002 – Operations Manual Volume 2: Raw Water Intake & Treatment.
- S03/OM/004 – Operations Manual Volume 4: Reservoirs & Distribution (under review).
- WQ/PR/07 – Water Quality Sampling and Analysis Procedure (DPD method).
- WQ/PR/12 – Calibration Procedure for On-line Chlorine Analysers.
- HS/PR/03 – Control of Substances Hazardous to Health (COSHH) – Chlorine.
- EM/PR/01 – Emergency Response Plan – Chlorine Gas Release.

2.2 Where a referenced document is superseded, the most recent version held by the Network Control Centre shall apply. Superseded versions are retained in the archive for audit purposes only and must not be used for operational decisions.

3. Chlorine Residual – Setpoints and Control Limits

Operations manual sets Cranwell TW Chlorination Unit chlorine residual setpoint at 0.9 mg/L. Record status: current.

3.1 The following table defines the chlorine residual setpoints and control limits for all treatment and distribution assets within the Aldercroft supply zone. Values are expressed as free chlorine in mg/L, measured at the point of sample.

Table 3.1 – Chlorine Residual Setpoints (Effective 2026-01-01)

3.2 The setpoint for the Cranwell TW Chlorination Unit final water is 0.9 mg/L. This value is the target for the automatic control loop and must be maintained at all times during normal operation. The setpoint is reviewed annually as part of the manual review cycle, and any proposed change must be supported by a Water Quality Risk Assessment and approved by the Water Quality Team Leader.

3.3 Control limits are provided as operational guidance. Operation outside the control limits does not automatically constitute a quality failure, provided the regulatory minimum of 0.2 mg/L at the customer tap is maintained. However, sustained operation above the upper control limit, or any excursion below the lower control limit for more than 30 minutes, must be reported to the Water Quality Team Leader and logged in the event log.

3.4 The on-line analyser at Cranwell TW is calibrated weekly against a grab sample analysed by DPD method. The calibration result must be within 0.05 mg/L of the grab sample value; if not, the analyser is taken out of service, and manual testing is implemented until calibration is successful.

3.5 For satellite re-chlorination points, the setpoint is maintained by local controllers. These controllers are checked monthly by the area technician, and the check must include a visual inspection of the dosing pump and a review of the residual trend for the preceding 7 days.
Table 4.1 – Disinfection Contact Time Requirements (Effective 2026-01-01)

4.2 The table above is effective from 2026-01-01 and supersedes all previously published contact time values. Superseded versions are retained in the archive for audit purposes only and must not be used for operational decisions.

4.3 Cranwell Treatment Works disinfection contact time is 22 minutes. This value is the minimum theoretical contact time that must be achieved at the peak hourly flow rate of 1.4 m³/s. The contact tank at Cranwell TW comprises two parallel compartments, each with a nominal volume of 925 m³, giving a combined volume of 1,850 m³ at the normal operating level of 4.2 m. The 22-minute value has been confirmed by the tracer study carried out on 2024-11-14, which used the fluoride tracer method, and the results were reviewed and accepted by the Water Quality Team Leader on 2024-12-02.

4.4 The CT value must be re-verified if any of the following occur:

a) A change to the peak hourly flow rate of more than 5% from the design value;
b) A change to the normal operating level of the contact tank;
c) Any modification to the inlet or outlet weirs, baffles, or pipework;
d) Any significant accumulation of sediment within the tank, as determined by the annual tank inspection;
e) A recommendation from the Water Quality Team Leader following an unsatisfactory tracer study or a water quality incident.

4.5 If the CT value is found to be below 22 minutes at any time, the flow to the contact tank must be reduced immediately, and the Water Quality Team Leader must be informed. The reduction in flow must be logged in the event log, and the reason for the reduction must be investigated before normal flow is restored.

Operations manual specifies Cranwell Treatment Works disinfection contact time as 22 minutes. Record status: current.

4.6 The contact tank at Cranwell TW is cleaned on a rolling programme, with each compartment cleaned every three years. The cleaning schedule is maintained by the Treatment Works Manager and is available in the site office. After cleaning, the tank is refilled and the CT value is re-verified by a dye test before the tank is returned to service. The dye test must be carried out at the same flow rate as the tracer study, and the results must be within 5% of the 22-minute value.

4.7 The on-line flow meter at the inlet to the contact tank is calibrated annually, and the calibration certificate is retained on file. The flow meter reading is compared to the sump pump run-time data on a weekly basis, and any discrepancy of more than 3% is investigated by the area technician.

4.9 The CT value for Marple Service Reservoir is 18 minutes. This value is based on the tracer study carried out on 2023-06-02. The reservoir has a single compartment with a volume of 820 m³ at the normal operating level. The CT value for Marple Service Reservoir is due for re-verification by tracer study no later than 2028-06-02, or earlier if any of the conditions in paragraph 4.4 apply.

4.11 All CT values in Table 4.1 are reviewed annually as part of the manual review cycle. Any proposed change to a CT value must be supported by a tracer study or a revised design calculation, and must be approved by the Water Quality Team Leader and the Treatment Works Manager. The approved change is recorded in the manual revision history, and the superseded value is retained in the archive for audit purposes only.
c) **Top water level:** The top water level is the maximum level to which the reservoir may be filled. Overfilling above the top water level may cause the air valve on the inlet to close, leading to pressure surge, and may also compromise the integrity of the roof slab. The level must not be allowed to exceed the top water level under any circumstances.

d) **Filling:** The reservoir is filled by the duty inlet valve at Cranwell TW. The valve is normally controlled by the level control system, which modulates the valve to maintain the reservoir level at the target level set in the telemetry system. The target level is normally set 0.3 m below the top water level. The target level may be adjusted by the Network Control Centre to manage water age, but must not be set below the minimum operating level plus 0.5 m without the approval of the Water Quality Team Leader.

e) **Emptying:** The reservoir is emptied through the outlet to the distribution network. There is no dedicated scour valve. If the reservoir needs to be taken out of service for inspection or maintenance, the outlet valve must be closed, and the reservoir must be isolated from the network. The procedure in Section 5.8 (Isolation for Inspection) must be followed.

f) **Level alarms:** The telemetry system is configured with two alarms for Hollowell Service Reservoir: a high level alarm at 0.1 m below the top water level, and a low level alarm at the minimum operating level. The alarms are monitored by the Network Control Centre on a 24-hour basis. On receipt of a low level alarm, the Network Control Centre must verify the level reading and, if confirmed, follow the procedure in Section 5.7.

**5.4 Table 5.1 – Service Reservoir Operating Setpoints**

The following table lists the operating setpoints for service reservoirs in the Aldercroft & District network. The table is reviewed annually as part of the manual review cycle. Any proposed change to a setpoint must be supported by a hydraulic analysis or a site investigation, and must be approved by the Network Control Manager and the Treatment Works Manager. The approved change is recorded in the manual revision history, and the superseded value is retained in the archive for audit purposes only.

| Reservoir | Location | Normal Operating Band (m) | Top Water Level (m) | Minimum Operating Level (m) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hollowell Service Reservoir | Hollowell, off Mill Lane | 3.2 – 6.4 | 6.4 | 3.2 | Single compartment. Level datum: floor of reservoir. |
| Marple Service Reservoir | Marple, adjacent to the old water tower | 2.1 – 5.8 | 5.8 | 2.1 | Two compartments, interconnected. See site schedule. |
| Cranwell Hill Service Reservoir | Cranwell, top of Beacon Hill | 1.8 – 4.9 | 4.9 | 1.8 | Covered reservoir. Level datum: floor of reservoir. |
| Lower Aldercroft Service Reservoir | Aldercroft, near the recreation ground | 2.5 – 5.2 | 5.2 | 2.5 | Single compartment. |

Reservoir operating rules set Hollowell Service Reservoir minimum operating level at 3.2 m. Record status: current. This value is current and was confirmed at the 2025 annual review. The value is also recorded in the site-specific operating schedule for Hollowell, held at the Northern Depot.

**5.5 Level Control – Cranwell Treatment Works to Hollowell Service Reservoir**

The level in Hollowell Service Reservoir is controlled by the duty inlet valve at Cranwell TW. The valve is a motorised butterfly valve, 150 mm diameter, located in the valve chamber at the outlet of the contact tank. The valve is controlled by the level control system, which uses the telemetry level reading from the reservoir as the process variable.
**5.6 Pumping Station Operation – Cranwell Hill Booster**

The Cranwell Hill Booster Station is located at the base of Beacon Hill, adjacent to the Cranwell Hill Service Reservoir access track. It receives water from the Lower Aldercroft zone and boosts it into the Cranwell Hill zone. The station is normally unmanned and is supervised via the Network Control Centre (NCC) telemetry system.

**5.6.1 Normal Duty Arrangement**

The station is equipped with two duty pumps (P1 and P2) and one standby pump (P3). Each pump is rated at 12 L/s against a total head of 28 m. The duty pump is selected by the automatic changeover sequence, which alternates the duty pump on a weekly basis. The changeover is scheduled to occur at 09:00 on a Monday morning, unless a pump is already running at that time to meet demand, in which case the changeover is deferred until the pump next stops.

The standby pump starts automatically if the running pump trips or if the discharge pressure falls below 0.8 bar for more than 10 seconds. The standby pump will also start if the wet well level at the booster station exceeds the high-level setpoint of 1.5 m, irrespective of the running pump status. This is a deliberate control logic decision to protect the wet well from flooding during periods of high inflow.

**5.6.2 Pump Start and Stop Setpoints**

The pump start and stop setpoints are controlled by the level in the Cranwell Hill Service Reservoir, not by the wet well level at the booster station. The wet well level is monitored for alarm purposes only, except in the case of the high-level override described in 5.6.1. The reservoir level setpoints are listed below.

| Pump Action | Reservoir Level (m) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Stop (all pumps) | 4.9 | Top water level. All pumps stop. |
| Stop (duty pump) | 4.6 | Duty pump stops. Standby will not start unless reservoir level falls again. |
| Start (duty pump) | 4.2 | Duty pump starts. |
| Start (standby pump) | 3.9 | Standby pump starts in addition to duty pump. |
| High-level alarm | 4.7 | Telemetry alarm to NCC. No automatic action. |
| Low-level alarm | 3.4 | Telemetry alarm to NCC. No automatic action. |

The setpoints in Table 5.2 are current and were confirmed at the 2025 annual review. Any proposed change must be supported by a hydraulic analysis and approved by the Network Control Manager.

**5.6.3 Pump Trip and Alarm Handling**

If a running pump trips, the standby pump will start automatically as described in 5.6.1. The trip event is logged by the local PLC and an alarm is raised to the NCC. The NCC operator will attempt to determine the cause of the trip from the telemetry data. If the cause is not immediately apparent, a field operator will be dispatched to the station.

Common causes of pump trips at Cranwell Hill include:

- Overload due to high discharge pressure (e.g., if a valve is closed downstream).
- Overheating of the motor, particularly during prolonged running at low flows.
- Loss of prime, which can occur if the suction line is partially blocked or if there is an air ingress in the suction pipework. This has been observed after heavy rainfall events when the wet well is subject to turbid inflow. Operators should check the suction strainer after such events.

If a pump trips due to a loss of prime, the pump must not be restarted remotely. The field operator must attend the station, inspect the suction line and strainer, and manually vent the pump casing before resetting the protection relay. A note to this effect is also recorded in the site log at the station.
**5.7 DISTRIBUTION ZONE MANAGEMENT**

**5.7.1 General**

The distribution network is divided into six pressure zones, each fed by a primary service reservoir or by direct pumping from a treatment works. The zones are listed in Table 5.3. Zone boundaries are defined by closed isolating valves; these valves must remain locked in the closed position unless a formal cross-zone transfer is authorised by the Network Control Centre (NCC).

| Zone Code | Zone Name | Primary Feed | Normal Operating Pressure (bar) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ZN-01 | Aldercroft Central | Cranwell Hill Service Reservoir | 3.2 – 4.1 |
| ZN-02 | East Aldercroft | Low Lift Pumping Station | 2.8 – 3.6 |
| ZN-03 | West Aldercroft | Cranwell Hill Service Reservoir | 3.5 – 4.4 |
| ZN-04 | Lower Brindle | Brindle Tower | 2.5 – 3.4 |
| ZN-05 | Upper Brindle | Brindle Tower (boosted) | 4.0 – 5.2 |
| ZN-06 | Marshfield | Marshfield Booster Station | 3.0 – 3.9 |

Pressures are monitored at permanent telemetry points at the zone boundaries and at a number of temporary loggers deployed for specific investigations. Pressure readings outside the normal band should be investigated promptly. A sustained low-pressure reading may indicate a burst, an open hydrant, or a failing pressure-reducing valve (PRV). A sustained high-pressure reading may indicate a faulty PRV or an incorrectly set control valve.

**5.7.2 Pressure Reducing Valves**

PRVs are installed at the following locations to manage pressures between zones:

- Aldercroft Central / East Aldercroft boundary – Marsh Lane PRV chamber.
- West Aldercroft / Lower Brindle boundary – Hilltop Road PRV chamber.
- Lower Brindle / Upper Brindle boundary – Brindle Rise PRV chamber.

Each PRV chamber is inspected on a six-monthly basis by the Distribution Maintenance Team. The inspection includes checking the valve for leakage, verifying the outlet pressure against the setpoint, and lubricating the adjusting screw. The setpoints for each PRV are held in the asset management system and are also displayed on a label inside the chamber lid.

If a PRV is found to be passing water when the downstream pressure is above the setpoint, the valve should be adjusted. If the valve cannot be adjusted to hold pressure, it should be scheduled for replacement. Any temporary adjustment to a PRV setpoint must be recorded in the site log and reported to the NCC at the next shift handover. A temporary adjustment should not be left in place for more than 14 days without a formal review.

**5.7.3 Valve Operations**

All valve operations on the distribution network must be carried out in accordance with the Valve Operations Procedure (ref. OP-DIST-004). This procedure covers the following points:

- Valves are identified by a unique asset number and a physical tag on the valve spindle.
- Before any valve is operated, the operator must confirm the valve identity and the direction of rotation to close. The direction of rotation is marked on the valve cover plate where possible.
- Valve spindles should be operated slowly to avoid pressure surges. A full turn should take at least 30 seconds.
- After operation, the valve position must be confirmed by visual inspection of the spindle indicator, where fitted, and the new position recorded in the valve log.

The NCC must be notified before any valve operation that may affect pressures or flows in a zone. This includes any operation on a valve that is more than 200 mm in diameter, or any operation that will isolate a section of main. For smaller valves, the operator should use their judgement, but should inform the NCC if the operation is likely to cause a visible change in flow or pressure.

- Satellite re-chlorination points at Aldercroft Hill, Lower Brampton, and the Marsh Lane booster.
- Manual chlorine residual testing (DPD method) at sample points throughout the distribution network.
- Calibration and verification of on-line chlorine analysers.
- Emergency procedures for loss of chlorination, chlorine gas escape, and contamination events.

1.3 For the purposes of this manual, "chlorine residual" refers to free chlorine, measured as mg/L, unless otherwise stated. Combined chlorine residuals are recorded separately and are not used for setpoint compliance.

2. References and Associated Documents

2.1 The following documents are referenced in this volume:
- S03/OM/001 – Operations Manual Volume 1: General Duties & Safety.
- S03/OM/002 – Operations Manual Volume 2: Raw Water Intake & Treatment.
- S03/OM/004 – Operations Manual Volume 4: Reservoirs & Distribution (under review).
- WQ/PR/07 – Water Quality Sampling and Analysis Procedure (DPD method).
- WQ/PR/12 – Calibration Procedure for On-line Chlorine Analysers.
- HS/PR/03 – Control of Substances Hazardous to Health (COSHH) – Chlorine.
- EM/PR/01 – Emergency Response Plan – Chlorine Gas Release.

2.2 Where a referenced document is superseded, the most recent version held by the Network Control Centre shall apply. Superseded versions are retained in the archive for audit purposes only and must not be used for operational decisions.

3. Chlorine Residual – Setpoints and Control Limits

Operations manual sets Cranwell TW Chlorination Unit chlorine residual setpoint at 0.9 mg/L. Record status: current.

3.1 The following table defines the chlorine residual setpoints and control limits for all treatment and distribution assets within the Aldercroft supply zone. Values are expressed as free chlorine in mg/L, measured at the point of sample.

Table 3.1 – Chlorine Residual Setpoints (Effective 2026-01-01)

3.2 The setpoint for the Cranwell TW Chlorination Unit final water is 0.9 mg/L. This value is the target for the automatic control loop and must be maintained at all times during normal operation. The setpoint is reviewed annually as part of the manual review cycle, and any proposed change must be supported by a Water Quality Risk Assessment and approved by the Water Quality Team Leader.

3.3 Control limits are provided as operational guidance. Operation outside the control limits does not automatically constitute a quality failure, provided the regulatory minimum of 0.2 mg/L at the customer tap is maintained. However, sustained operation above the upper control limit, or any excursion below the lower control limit for more than 30 minutes, must be reported to the Water Quality Team Leader and logged in the event log.

3.4 The on-line analyser at Cranwell TW is calibrated weekly against a grab sample analysed by DPD method. The calibration result must be within 0.05 mg/L of the grab sample value; if not, the analyser is taken out of service, and manual testing is implemented until calibration is successful.

3.5 For satellite re-chlorination points, the setpoint is maintained by local controllers. These controllers are checked monthly by the area technician, and the check must include a visual inspection of the dosing pump and a review of the residual trend for the preceding 7 days.

4.2 The table above is effective from 2026-01-01 and supersedes all previously published contact time values. Superseded versions are retained in the archive for audit purposes only and must not be used for operational decisions.

4.3 Cranwell Treatment Works disinfection contact time is 22 minutes. This value is the minimum theoretical contact time that must be achieved at the peak hourly flow rate of 1.4 m³/s. The contact tank at Cranwell TW comprises two parallel compartments, each with a nominal volume of 925 m³, giving a combined volume of 1,850 m³ at the normal operating level of 4.2 m. The 22-minute value has been confirmed by the tracer study carried out on 2024-11-14, which used the fluoride tracer method, and the results were reviewed and accepted by the Water Quality Team Leader on 2024-12-02.

4.4 The CT value must be re-verified if any of the following occur:

a) A change to the peak hourly flow rate of more than 5% from the design value;
b) A change to the normal operating level of the contact tank;
c) Any modification to the inlet or outlet weirs, baffles, or pipework;
d) Any significant accumulation of sediment within the tank, as determined by the annual tank inspection;
e) A recommendation from the Water Quality Team Leader following an unsatisfactory tracer study or a water quality incident.

4.5 If the CT value is found to be below 22 minutes at any time, the flow to the contact tank must be reduced immediately, and the Water Quality Team Leader must be informed. The reduction in flow must be logged in the event log, and the reason for the reduction must be investigated before normal flow is restored.

Operations manual specifies Cranwell Treatment Works disinfection contact time as 22 minutes. Record status: current.

4.6 The contact tank at Cranwell TW is cleaned on a rolling programme, with each compartment cleaned every three years. The cleaning schedule is maintained by the Treatment Works Manager and is available in the site office. After cleaning, the tank is refilled and the CT value is re-verified by a dye test before the tank is returned to service. The dye test must be carried out at the same flow rate as the tracer study, and the results must be within 5% of the 22-minute value.

4.7 The on-line flow meter at the inlet to the contact tank is calibrated annually, and the calibration certificate is retained on file. The flow meter reading is compared to the sump pump run-time data on a weekly basis, and any discrepancy of more than 3% is investigated by the area technician.

4.9 The CT value for Marple Service Reservoir is 18 minutes. This value is based on the tracer study carried out on 2023-06-02. The reservoir has a single compartment with a volume of 820 m³ at the normal operating level. The CT value for Marple Service Reservoir is due for re-verification by tracer study no later than 2028-06-02, or earlier if any of the conditions in paragraph 4.4 apply.

4.11 All CT values in Table 4.1 are reviewed annually as part of the manual review cycle. Any proposed change to a CT value must be supported by a tracer study or a revised design calculation, and must be approved by the Water Quality Team Leader and the Treatment Works Manager. The approved change is recorded in the manual revision history, and the superseded value is retained in the archive for audit purposes only.

c) **Top water level:** The top water level is the maximum level to which the reservoir may be filled. Overfilling above the top water level may cause the air valve on the inlet to close, leading to pressure surge, and may also compromise the integrity of the roof slab. The level must not be allowed to exceed the top water level under any circumstances.

d) **Filling:** The reservoir is filled by the duty inlet valve at Cranwell TW. The valve is normally controlled by the level control system, which modulates the valve to maintain the reservoir level at the target level set in the telemetry system. The target level is normally set 0.3 m below the top water level. The target level may be adjusted by the Network Control Centre to manage water age, but must not be set below the minimum operating level plus 0.5 m without the approval of the Water Quality Team Leader.

e) **Emptying:** The reservoir is emptied through the outlet to the distribution network. There is no dedicated scour valve. If the reservoir needs to be taken out of service for inspection or maintenance, the outlet valve must be closed, and the reservoir must be isolated from the network. The procedure in Section 5.8 (Isolation for Inspection) must be followed.

f) **Level alarms:** The telemetry system is configured with two alarms for Hollowell Service Reservoir: a high level alarm at 0.1 m below the top water level, and a low level alarm at the minimum operating level. The alarms are monitored by the Network Control Centre on a 24-hour basis. On receipt of a low level alarm, the Network Control Centre must verify the level reading and, if confirmed, follow the procedure in Section 5.7.

The level in Hollowell Service Reservoir is controlled by the duty inlet valve at Cranwell TW. **5.6 Pumping Station Operation – Cranwell Hill Booster**

The Cranwell Hill Booster Station is located at the base of Beacon Hill, adjacent to the Cranwell Hill Service Reservoir access track. It receives water from the Lower Aldercroft zone and boosts it into the Cranwell Hill zone. The station is normally unmanned and is supervised via the Network Control Centre (NCC) telemetry system.

**5.6.1 Normal Duty Arrangement**

The station is equipped with two duty pumps (P1 and P2) and one standby pump (P3). Each pump is rated at 12 L/s against a total head of 28 m. The duty pump is selected by the automatic changeover sequence, which alternates the duty pump on a weekly basis. The changeover is scheduled to occur at 09:00 on a Monday morning, unless a pump is already running at that time to meet demand, in which case the changeover is deferred until the pump next stops.

The standby pump starts automatically if the running pump trips or if the discharge pressure falls below 0.8 bar for more than 10 seconds. The standby pump will also start if the wet well level at the booster station exceeds the high-level setpoint of 1.5 m, irrespective of the running pump status. This is a deliberate control logic decision to protect the wet well from flooding during periods of high inflow.

**5.6.2 Pump Start and Stop Setpoints**

The pump start and stop setpoints are controlled by the level in the Cranwell Hill Service Reservoir, not by the wet well level at the booster station. The wet well level is monitored for alarm purposes only, except in the case of the high-level override described in 5.6.1. The reservoir level setpoints are listed below.

| Pump Action | Reservoir Level (m) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Stop (all pumps) | 4.9 | Top water level. All pumps stop. |
| Stop (duty pump) | 4.6 | Duty pump stops. Standby will not start unless reservoir level falls again. |
| Start (duty pump) | 4.2 | Duty pump starts. |
| Start (standby pump) | 3.9 | Standby pump starts in addition to duty pump. |
| High-level alarm | 4.7 | Telemetry alarm to NCC. No automatic action. |
| Low-level alarm | 3.4 | Telemetry alarm to NCC. No automatic action. |

The setpoints in Table 5.2 are current and were confirmed at the 2025 annual review. Any proposed change must be supported by a hydraulic analysis and approved by the Network Control Manager.

**5.6.3 Pump Trip and Alarm Handling**

If a running pump trips, the standby pump will start automatically as described in 5.6.1. The trip event is logged by the local PLC and an alarm is raised to the NCC. The NCC operator will attempt to determine the cause of the trip from the telemetry data. If the cause is not immediately apparent, a field operator will be dispatched to the station.

Common causes of pump trips at Cranwell Hill include:

- Overload due to high discharge pressure (e.g., if a valve is closed downstream).
- Overheating of the motor, particularly during prolonged running at low flows.
- Loss of prime, which can occur if the suction line is partially blocked or if there is an air ingress in the suction pipework. This has been observed after heavy rainfall events when the wet well is subject to turbid inflow. Operators should check the suction strainer after such events.

If a pump trips due to a loss of prime, the pump must not be restarted remotely. The field operator must attend the station, inspect the suction line and strainer, and manually vent the pump casing before resetting the protection relay. A note to this effect is also recorded in the site log at the station.

**5.7 DISTRIBUTION ZONE MANAGEMENT**

**5.7.1 General**

The distribution network is divided into six pressure zones, each fed by a primary service reservoir or by direct pumping from a treatment works. The zones are listed in Table 5.3. Zone boundaries are defined by closed isolating valves; these valves must remain locked in the closed position unless a formal cross-zone transfer is authorised by the Network Control Centre (NCC).

| Zone Code | Zone Name | Primary Feed | Normal Operating Pressure (bar) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ZN-01 | Aldercroft Central | Cranwell Hill Service Reservoir | 3.2 – 4.1 |
| ZN-02 | East Aldercroft | Low Lift Pumping Station | 2.8 – 3.6 |
| ZN-03 | West Aldercroft | Cranwell Hill Service Reservoir | 3.5 – 4.4 |
| ZN-04 | Lower Brindle | Brindle Tower | 2.5 – 3.4 |
| ZN-05 | Upper Brindle | Brindle Tower (boosted) | 4.0 – 5.2 |
| ZN-06 | Marshfield | Marshfield Booster Station | 3.0 – 3.9 |

Pressures are monitored at permanent telemetry points at the zone boundaries and at a number of temporary loggers deployed for specific investigations. Pressure readings outside the normal band should be investigated promptly. A sustained low-pressure reading may indicate a burst, an open hydrant, or a failing pressure-reducing valve (PRV). A sustained high-pressure reading may indicate a faulty PRV or an incorrectly set control valve.

**5.7.2 Pressure Reducing Valves**

PRVs are installed at the following locations to manage pressures between zones:

- Aldercroft Central / East Aldercroft boundary – Marsh Lane PRV chamber.
- West Aldercroft / Lower Brindle boundary – Hilltop Road PRV chamber.
- Lower Brindle / Upper Brindle boundary – Brindle Rise PRV chamber.

Each PRV chamber is inspected on a six-monthly basis by the Distribution Maintenance Team. The inspection includes checking the valve for leakage, verifying the outlet pressure against the setpoint, and lubricating the adjusting screw. The setpoints for each PRV are held in the asset management system and are also displayed on a label inside the chamber lid.

If a PRV is found to be passing water when the downstream pressure is above the setpoint, the valve should be adjusted. If the valve cannot be adjusted to hold pressure, it should be scheduled for replacement. Any temporary adjustment to a PRV setpoint must be recorded in the site log and reported to the NCC at the next shift handover. A temporary adjustment should not be left in place for more than 14 days without a formal review.

**5.7.3 Valve Operations**

All valve operations on the distribution network must be carried out in accordance with the Valve Operations Procedure (ref. OP-DIST-004). This procedure covers the following points:

- Valves are identified by a unique asset number and a physical tag on the valve spindle.
- Before any valve is operated, the operator must confirm the valve identity and the direction of rotation to close. The direction of rotation is marked on the valve cover plate where possible.
- Valve spindles should be operated slowly to avoid pressure surges. A full turn should take at least 30 seconds.
- After operation, the valve position must be confirmed by visual inspection of the spindle indicator, where fitted, and the new position recorded in the valve log.

The NCC must be notified before any valve operation that may affect pressures or flows in a zone. This includes any operation on a valve that is more than 200 mm in diameter, or any operation that will isolate a section of main. For smaller valves, the operator should use their judgement, but should inform the NCC if the operation is likely to cause a visible change in flow or pressure.
